questions.question: A normal-form game is a triple $G=\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle$ with players $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, nonempty pure-strategy sets $S_i$ and profile set $S=S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$. On which set is player $i$'s payoff function $v_i$ defined?
options: On $S_i$: it assigns a number to each of player $i$'s strategies.
On $N$: it assigns a number to each player.
On $S$, with a vector of all players' payoffs as value.
On $S$: it assigns a real number to every strategy profile.

questions.question: A normal-form game requires every pure-strategy set $S_i$ to be nonempty. In a two-player model, suppose $S_1=\{T,B\}$ but $S_2=\varnothing$. What is the profile set $S=S_1\times S_2$?
options: $S_1$, since a factor without strategies is simply ignored
$\varnothing$, since no profile can list a strategy for player 2
$S_1\times\{\varnothing\}$, with player 2 choosing the empty set
$S_1\cup S_2=S_1$, the union of the two strategy sets

questions.question: A normal-form game is a triple $G=\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle$ with players $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, nonempty pure-strategy sets $S_i$ and profile set $S=S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$. What is an element of the set $S$?
options: One strategy $s_i\in S_i$ for each player, listed in order
A single strategy chosen by one of the players
The set $S_i$ of all strategies of one player
A list $(v_1(s),\ldots,v_n(s))$ of payoffs

questions.question: For a two-player normal-form game with payoff functions $v_1,v_2$ on the profile set $S$, when is the game called zero-sum?
options: When $v_1(s)+v_2(s)=0$ for at least one profile $s\in S$
When the payoffs of all profiles sum to zero for each player
When $v_1(s)+v_2(s)=0$ for every profile $s\in S$
When both players always receive equal payoffs

questions.question: A two-player normal-form game has $S_1=S_2$. Which further condition makes it symmetric?
options: $v_1(a,b)=v_2(b,a)$ for all strategies $a,b$
$v_1(a,b)=v_2(a,b)$ for all strategies $a,b$
$v_1(a,b)=v_1(b,a)$ for all strategies $a,b$
$v_1(a,b)=-v_2(b,a)$ for all strategies $a,b$

questions.question: Player 1 chooses row $U$ or $D$, player 2 column $L$ or $R$, and each cell lists $(v_1,v_2)$: row $U$: $L$: $(5,-1)$, $R$: $(2,3)$; row $D$: $L$: $(0,4)$, $R$: $(-2,1)$. What are $v_1(D,L)$ and $v_2(D,L)$?
A normal-form game has three players with $2$, $3$ and $4$ pure strategies. How many payoff numbers are needed to describe all payoff functions $v_1,v_2,v_3$?
A two-player game has cells $(v_1,v_2)$: $(T,L)=(2,-2)$, $(T,R)=(-1,1)$, $(B,L)=(0,0)$, $(B,R)=(3,-2)$. Is it zero-sum?
options: No: at $(B,R)$ the payoffs sum to $1$.
Yes: three of the four cells sum to zero.
Yes: at $(B,L)$ both players get $0$.
No: at $(B,L)$ neither player gains.

questions.question: A game has $S_1=S_2=\{A,B\}$ and payoffs $(v_1,v_2)$: $(A,A)=(3,3)$, $(A,B)=(0,5)$, $(B,A)=(5,0)$, $(B,B)=(1,1)$. A game is symmetric if $v_1(a,b)=v_2(b,a)$ for all $a,b$. Is this game symmetric?
options: No: $v_1(A,B)=0$ differs from $v_2(A,B)=5$.
Yes: for instance $v_1(A,B)=0=v_2(B,A)$.
No: the cells $(A,B)$ and $(B,A)$ differ.
Yes, since it is a zero-sum game.

questions.question: A normal-form game is a triple $G=\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle$ with players $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, nonempty pure-strategy sets $S_i$ and profile set $S=S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$. Can a player's strategy set be an interval such as $S_i=[0,\infty)$?
options: No: a normal-form game needs finitely many strategies.
Yes, but only if each payoff function is constant.
No: payoffs cannot be defined on infinite sets.
Yes: the game is then given by payoff formulas, not a matrix.

questions.question: A normal-form game is a triple $G=\langle N,\{S_i\},\{v_i\}\rangle$ with players $N=\{1,\ldots,n\}$, nonempty pure-strategy sets $S_i$ and profile set $S=S_1\times\cdots\times S_n$. A modeller writes down payoffs only for the profiles she expects to be played. Does this define a normal-form game?
options: Yes: payoffs of unplayed profiles do not affect anything.
Yes, provided each player has at least one listed profile.
No: each $v_i$ must give a payoff at every profile in $S$.
Yes, if the expected profiles are common knowledge among the players.

questions.question: In a two-player zero-sum game, $v_1(s)+v_2(s)=0$ for every profile $s$. Which statement about writing the game as a matrix is correct?
options: Both numbers are still needed, as $v_2$ is unrelated to $v_1$.
One number per row suffices, as rows sum to zero.
One number per cell, player 1's payoff, determines the whole game.
The matrix must contain only zeros, as payoffs sum to zero.

questions.question: Two players choose $s_1,s_2\in[0,5]$; the payoff functions are $v_1(s_1,s_2)=s_1(4-s_2)$ and $v_2(s_1,s_2)=s_2(s_1-1)$. At the profile $(s_1,s_2)=(2,3)$, what is player 2's payoff?

A static game of complete information is one in which players choose simultaneously, nobody observes another's choice first, and the players, actions and payoffs are common knowledge. Why does a normal-form game describe such a game completely?
options: No choice is observed first, so each strategy is simply an action.
Because the payoffs are common knowledge, which the normal form lists.
Because players choose at the same clock time, so order is irrelevant.
Because static games always have finitely many actions.

questions.question: A two-player game with $S_1=S_2$ is both symmetric, $v_1(a,b)=v_2(b,a)$ for all $a,b$, and zero-sum, $v_1(s)+v_2(s)=0$ for all profiles $s$. What must $v_1(a,a)$ be for every strategy $a$?
options: It can be any number
$-v_1(a,a)$, a different number

questions.question: In rock-paper-scissors, $S_1=S_2=\{R,P,S\}$; a win (rock beats scissors, scissors beat paper, paper beats rock) pays the winner $1$ and the loser $-1$, and a tie pays $0$ to both. Which properties does the game have?
options: Only zero-sum: payoffs within a cell differ.
Only symmetric: ties give both players $0$.
Neither: ties break both properties.
It is both symmetric and zero-sum.

questions.question: A symmetric two-player game, $v_1(a,b)=v_2(b,a)$ for all $a,b$, has $S_1=S_2$ with $4$ strategies each. How many numbers are needed to determine both payoff functions?
